[Projectile — Behavior priority and Interactions] Whenever a projectile collides, it will attempt each of its remaining behaviors
Projectile behaviors occur in the following order, if applicable:
Split
Pierce
Fork
Chain
For example:
A projectile first hits a target and splits towards a second target.
The projectile pierces the next N targets.
If a projectile can pierce indefinitely, further behaviors will never activate.
Terrain cannot be pierced.
The next target on its path that does not get pierced causes the projectile to fork into two projectiles.
The forked projectiles then chain N times until no valid targets remain or chaining is exhausted.
Different behaviors cannot occur simultaneously; the priority order determines how they occur.

[Projectile — Behaviours] Projectile behaviours follow a specific order:
Cannot Collide: Prevents projectiles from hitting enemies while in flight and prevents other behavours. Projectiles can still hit the enemy if they have an area of effect component that either do not require collision or occurs when hitting the ground or terrain (e.g. walls).
Split: Causes projectiles to each fire towards multiple targets within 6 metres after hitting an initial target.
Split projectiles that have no valid targets will fire in random directions.
Pierce: Allows projectiles to continue their trajectory after hitting an entity on their path.
Piercing can occur up to N times. Each pierce has an independent chance to occur.
Fork: Causes projectiles to create two copies upon hitting a target.
These copies are fired at a fixed angle from the target hit by the original projectile.
Chain: Redirects a single projectile to the nearest target within chain range that has not been hit by other projectiles from the same group.
Chaining can occur up to N times per projectile.

[Evasion — Entropy] Evasion is not a random system. Instead, it uses a deterministic "entropy" system that ensures a hit will occur after a certain number of evades:
If it is the first time an entity is attacked, or if the time since the last attempted hit exceeds 100 server ticks (3.33 seconds), randomize the entropy value from 0-99.
Calculate the attacker's chance to hit against the defender's chance to evade, and add this integer to the entropy value.
If the resulting entropy value is lower than 100, the hit counts as evade. When the value reaches 100 or greater, the check counts as a hit, and subtract 100 from the entropy value.
The secondary critical hit downgrade test does not affect the entropy value.
As a result, if a player has a 1 in N chance to be hit, then the player will be hit exactly once for every N consecutive attacks. This eliminates all possibilities of lucky and/or unlucky streaks. It is still based on chance because of the entropy's value randomization in the first step. Note that if multiple mobs are attacking one character, all of the mobs' attacks share the same entropy value. The chance to evade shown in the character stats window is based on the average accuracy of a monster at the player's level.

[Gem — Corruption] Corrupting a skill gem can cause it to gain or lose a skill level, gem socket, or quality.
Corruption effects that add or subtract a gem level are innate to the skill gem and works independently from the gem's actual level.

[Ghost Dance — Overview] Ghost Dance is a persistent buff skill. It periodically grants a stack of Ghost Shroud. Upon taking a hit, a stack of Ghost Shroud is consumed to recover energy shield based on your Evasion Rating.

[Critical hit — Critical hit check] When a skill is used or triggered, it performs a critical hit check by rolling a number. This roll ranges from 0 to 99.99, determining a threshold the skill's critical hit chance must exceed to deal a critical hit successfully.
For example: A player casts a spell and rolls a 12. When enemies are hit, those hits require a critical strike chance of 12.01% or greater to deal a critical hit.
While hits from the same skill will usually have the same critical hit chance, resulting in all-or-nothing behaviour, conditional modifiers and buffs/debuffs can cause critical hit chance to differ between enemies.
Critical hits are rolled for all hits from that skill. If a critical hit chance roll succeeds, all hits from that skill will be a critical hit.
This does not apply to Sustained and Channelling skills which hit continuously while channelling. Sustained skill will roll critical hit chance for each hit individually, and channelling skills will roll critical hit chance for each cast interval of the channelled skill.
Multi-projectile skills from players and allies roll crit independently, but projectiles from a monster's skill will either all crit or not crit.
If critical hit chance is lucky, skills perform two crit checks and keep the lower requirement. If it is unlucky, the higher requirement is kept.

Enemy's Heavy Stun buildup can be seen as a bar under their Life bar. Heavy Stun buildup decreases over time if the target has not had any Heavy Stun buildup applied to them for a certain period of time, or rapidly after a Heavy Stun animation finishes.
Cold damage cannot build up Heavy Stun (it applies Chill and build up Freeze instead).
Physical damage, and player (but not monster) Melee Damage, each cause 50% more Heavy Stun buildup. For players, these bonuses are multiplicative with each other (for a combined 125% more Heavy Stun buildup).

[Stun — Heavy stun] When a target's Heavy Stun threshold is reached (when a target's Stun buildup is filled), it goes into a longer stun animation; the duration of the heavy stun depends on the specific monster. The Duration of an inflicted Stun is based on the Damage dealt by the Hit relative to the target's Stun Threshold, with higher Damage Hits resulting in longer Stuns. Heavy Stunned targets are considered to be Immobilised. Heavy Stun buildup cannot occur while the target is Heavy Stunned or while Heavy Stun buildup empties after a Heavy Stun animation finishes. After inflicting a Heavy Stun, it becomes harder to apply more Heavy Stun to the target.
Player minions cannot be Heavy Stunned unless otherwise specified.

[Stun — Stun threshold] Stun threshold modifies the amount of stun buildup needed to inflict a stun. Increasing stun threshold reduces the chance of receiving a light stun and the amount of heavy stun accumulated, and vice versa.
Players have a base Stun Threshold value equal to their maximum life.

[Stun — Interaction with damage types] Physical damage and melee hits are more effective at applying stun.
For players, both physical damage and melee hits have 50% more chance to apply Light Stun and 50% more Heavy Stun buildup. These bonuses are multiplicative, meaning a physical melee hit is 125% more effective at stunning than damage types of neither.
For monsters, melee attacks have 33% more Light Stun chance and Heavy Stun buildup, and physical damage has 100% more. These bonuses are also multiplicative, meaning monster melee physical hits have 166% more chance to stun than hits of neither.

[Energy Shield — Damage mitigation] Energy shield protects life by being depleted first before taking damage to life.
The damage inflicted on Energy Shield is calculated after all damage mitigation factors, such as physical or elemental resistances, have been taken into account.
Damage from Bleeding and Poison bypass energy shield, damaging life directly. Certain items may also cause damage to bypass energy shield.
Chaos damage removes twice as much energy shield as other damage types. This does not affect the overall damage dealt. In the case that Chaos Damage deals damage to both Energy Shield and Life (or Mana) in a single instance of damage, it will not affect the Life or Mana removed.

[Chaos — Mechanics] Chaos damage is somewhat rarer than the other damage types, and is more often seen as damage over time rather than hit damage. It is stronger against energy shield, but a character with Chaos Inoculation is completely immune to chaos damage.
Chaos damage is usually used alongside Withered, a stacking debuff that increases chaos damage taken.

Each point near the cap removes a larger share of the remaining damage, so the last few percent to the cap are worth more than they look. Uncapped elemental resistance is the most common avoidable cause of deaths, so the planner fixes it before buying damage.
Chaos resistance usually starts at 0% and is not covered by "all elemental resistances" modifiers. It deserves more weight for energy-shield characters, because chaos damage removes twice as much energy shield (wiki: Energy Shield, Chaos). Characters with Chaos Inoculation are immune to chaos damage, so chaos resistance is irrelevant for them.

[Chaos — Overview] Chaos damage is one of the five damage types. It can be mitigated by chaos resistance. Chaos damage has the effect of removing twice as much energy shield when dealing damage.

[Chaos Inoculation — Mechanics] CI grants immunity to chaos damage, therefore causing the player to be unaffected by poison or other chaos damage over time effects. It also grants immunity to bleeding. It does not prevent Corrupted Blood or other physical damage over time sources.
The player's stun and ailment thresholds will be based on the new value of 1 maximum life, instead of being based on the amount of maximum life you would have without this keystone. It is recommended to take passives that grant additional stun and ailment threshold based on your energy shield to counteract them.
While CI is allocated, a player always counts as being on full life but can never be on low life.
Any effects that cause damage to bypass your energy shield (e.g. Heavy Buffer notable) will cause you to die instantly on taking damage if not fully redirected (e.g. Mind over Matter). Additionally, life loss effects will cause death if not countered with an equivalent amount of life regeneration; however, this can still result in death due to effects that disable or reduce life regeneration/recovery.

[Mind Over Matter — Mechanics] All damage that would be inflicted on the character's life is deducted from mana instead. If the character has insufficient mana, then the remainder of the damage will be taken from life.
As Mind Over Matter does not actually reduce total incoming damage or increase the player's actual life total, it does not affect the threshold or effectiveness of stun and ailments applied to players.
When combined with Chaos Inoculation, both energy shield and mana must be depleted before any damage affects life.
If both Chaos Inoculation and Eldritch Battery are taken, the player must fully deplete the enhanced mana pool before taking any damage to life. The player will still be technically immune to Bleeding as they will take all damage to mana first before life.
In the Trial of the Sekhemas, Mind over Matter will cause the player's maximum mana to be added to their total Honour, in addition to life and energy shield.

[Ailment — Ailment and Poise Thresholds] Player ailment threshold is based on half of their maximum life by default, though modifiers can cause it to also scale from other stats such as Energy Shield or Mana instead.

[Ailment — Mechanics] The chance for most ailments to be applied generally depends on the amount of damage dealt before mitigation compared to the defender's ailment threshold value. A player's base ailment threshold is based on half of their maximum life. This scaling is different for monsters; monster ailment threshold scales with monster level and is independent of monster life. Immobilization effects, such as freeze, electrocute, pin and stun use a different value called "poise". Both of these values have their own multiplier depending on rarity of the monster .
Chill will always be applied as long as the damage meets the minimum ailment threshold to not be discarded, though its slow magnitude scales with the ailment threshold formula.
The chance to inflict poison or bleeding is based on a static numerical chance instead rather than being calculated via the ailment threshold formula.
The chance to inflict an ailment is multiplicative against the chance to avoid an ailment. If the defender has 100% chance to avoid an ailment, they cannot be inflicted with that ailment, even by constant ground effects that usually bypass ailment avoidance chance.

Enemy's Heavy Stun buildup can be seen as a bar under their Life bar. Heavy Stun buildup decreases over time if the target has not had any Heavy Stun buildup applied to them for a certain period of time, or rapidly after a Heavy Stun animation finishes.

[Stun — Heavy stun] When a target's Heavy Stun threshold is reached (when a target's Stun buildup is filled), it goes into a longer stun animation; the duration of the heavy stun depends on the specific monster. The Duration of an inflicted Stun is based on the Damage dealt by the Hit relative to the target's Stun Threshold, with higher Damage Hits resulting in longer Stuns. Heavy Stunned targets are considered to be Immobilised. Heavy Stun buildup cannot occur while the target is Heavy Stunned or while Heavy Stun buildup empties after a Heavy Stun animation finishes. After inflicting a Heavy Stun, it becomes harder to apply more Heavy Stun to the target.
Player minions cannot be Heavy Stunned unless otherwise specified.

[Stun — Interaction with damage types] Physical damage and melee hits are more effective at applying stun.
For players, both physical damage and melee hits have 50% more chance to apply Light Stun and 50% more Heavy Stun buildup. These bonuses are multiplicative, meaning a physical melee hit is 125% more effective at stunning than damage types of neither.
For monsters, melee attacks have 33% more Light Stun chance and Heavy Stun buildup, and physical damage has 100% more. These bonuses are also multiplicative, meaning monster melee physical hits have 166% more chance to stun than hits of neither.

[Stun — Stun threshold] Stun threshold modifies the amount of stun buildup needed to inflict a stun. Increasing stun threshold reduces the chance of receiving a light stun and the amount of heavy stun accumulated, and vice versa.
Players have a base Stun Threshold value equal to their maximum life.

retrieved_contexts:
[Armour — Rule of thumb] To prevent one third of damage (33%), you need armour 5 times the damage (e.g. 500 armour for 100 damage)
To prevent half of damage (50%), you need armour 10 times the damage (e.g. 1000 armour for 100 damage)
To prevent two thirds of damage (66%), you need armour 20 times the damage (e.g. 2000 armour for 100 damage)
To prevent three quarters of damage (75%), you need armour 30 times the damage (e.g. 3000 armour for 100 damage)
To prevent 90% of damage, you need armour 90 times the damage (e.g. 9000 armour for 100 damage)
When the damage of a hit significantly exceeds Armour, it will never prevent more damage than the armour value divided by 10 (e.g. 1000 armour will never prevent more than 100 damage at its minimum percentage prevention).

[Armour — Mechanics] Armour grants physical damage reduction, with the exact amount of damage reduction depending on the ratio of armour to the physical damage of the hit. If the armour value is significantly larger than the damage, most of the damage is prevented. If the armour value is similar to or less than the incoming damage, only a small percentage of that damage will be prevented. As a result, armour is more effective against many smaller hits rather than fewer larger hits, even if the total damage dealt would be identical.
Armour never mitigates damage over time, as armour only applies to hits. Bleed is an ailment that deals physical damage over time that is based on the physical damage dealt by a skill before mitigation; armour will reduce the hit damage but not the damage over time. However, both the hit damage and the damage over time can be mitigated with sources of #% additional Physical Damage Reduction. The maximum total physical damage reduction from all sources is 90%.

[Deflection — Overview] Deflection is type of mitigation. It grants a chance to take less damage from a hit by a percentage. Like Evasion, chance to deflect is based on the defender's Deflection Rating against the attacker's Accuracy Rating. Most sources of Deflection Rating scale with the user's Evasion Rating, acting as a supplementary mitigation tool for evasion-based builds.

[Bleeding — Mechanics] Bleeding deals 75% of a hit's physical damage dealt (before mitigation and damage taken modifiers) as physical damage over time over 5 seconds. Bleeding on monsters (not players) deal an extra 100% damage while the target is moving, or if the bleeding is Aggravated. This percentage is affected multiplicatively by ailment magnitude. Ailment damage cannot be scaled directly; however, it can be indirectly scaled by modifying the hit damage.
Bleeding does not stack; each instance of bleeding has an independent duration and only the highest damage instance of bleeding will deal damage.
Bleeding chance depends on an explicit chance to inflict Bleeding.
The damage over time from bleeding bypasses energy shield and damages life directly. It also cannot be redirected to another resource, such as to Mana with Mind Over Matter.
Note that bleeding can be applied by any skill that can hit, not exclusively attacks.

[Damage conversion — Overconversion] If conversion in either step exceeds 100% of an original damage type, the conversion is normalized to 100%. For example, if a character converts 100% of physical damage to cold damage and 50% of physical damage to fire damage through item modifiers only, the conversion will be at a ratio of 67%/33% of physical damage as cold/fire instead.

[Projectile — Behavior priority and Interactions] Whenever a projectile collides, it will attempt each of its remaining behaviors
Projectile behaviors occur in the following order, if applicable:
Split
Pierce
Fork
Chain
For example:
A projectile first hits a target and splits towards a second target.
The projectile pierces the next N targets.
If a projectile can pierce indefinitely, further behaviors will never activate.
Terrain cannot be pierced.
The next target on its path that does not get pierced causes the projectile to fork into two projectiles.
The forked projectiles then chain N times until no valid targets remain or chaining is exhausted.
Different behaviors cannot occur simultaneously; the priority order determines how they occur.

[Projectile — Behaviours] Projectile behaviours follow a specific order:
Cannot Collide: Prevents projectiles from hitting enemies while in flight and prevents other behavours. Projectiles can still hit the enemy if they have an area of effect component that either do not require collision or occurs when hitting the ground or terrain (e.g. walls).
Split: Causes projectiles to each fire towards multiple targets within 6 metres after hitting an initial target.
Split projectiles that have no valid targets will fire in random directions.
Pierce: Allows projectiles to continue their trajectory after hitting an entity on their path.
Piercing can occur up to N times. Each pierce has an independent chance to occur.
Fork: Causes projectiles to create two copies upon hitting a target.
These copies are fired at a fixed angle from the target hit by the original projectile.
Chain: Redirects a single projectile to the nearest target within chain range that has not been hit by other projectiles from the same group.
Chaining can occur up to N times per projectile.
